etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English greven, from Old French grever (“to burden”), from Latin gravō, gravāre, from adjective gravis (“grave”). For the meaning development compare with Russian тяготи́ть (tjagotítʹ, “to be a burden (on), to oppress”), Russian тужи́ть (tužítʹ, “to experience grief”), related to Russian тяжёлый (tjažólyj, “heavy, grave”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause sorrow or distress to.

quote.citation: 1782, William Cowper, “On the Receipt of my Mother’s Picture”, in Poems, London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Thy maidens griev'd themselves at my concern.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To feel very sad about; to mourn; to sorrow for.
(transitive) To submit or file a grievance (about).

quote.citation: 2009, D'Amico, Rob (editor), Texas Teacher, published by Texas AFT (affiliate of American Federation of Teachers, AFL-CIO); "Austin classified employees gain due process rights", April 2009, p14:
quote.text: Even if the executive director rules against the employee on appeal, the employee can still grieve the termination to the superintendent followed by an appeal to the [...] Board of Trustees.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English greve, greyve, grave, grafe, from Old Norse greifi, from Middle Low German grēve, grâve, related to Old English grœfa, groefa, variants of Old English ġerēfa (“steward, reeve”). More at reeve.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A governor of a town or province.
(chiefly Scotland) A manager or steward, e.g. of a farm.

quote.citation: 1815 February 24, [Walter Scott], Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […]  James Ballantyne and Co. for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, […]; and Archibald Constable and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Their children were horsewhipped by the grieve.
